lessons.title: Follow a value through a program

blocks.text: A name remembers a value
Python runs these statements in order. Assigning subtotal to total copies the reference to the current number. Reassigning subtotal later does not recalculate total.

cases.label: Before a price change
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6

cases.label: Recalculate the total
cases.code:
price = 4
total = price * 3
price = 6
total = price * 3

blocks.text: Running again changes state
A notebook kernel keeps names between cell runs. Repeating a cell containing += updates the existing value again. Its position on the page does not tell you how often it ran.

cases.label: One update
cases.code:
count = 2
count += 3
print(count)

cases.label: Two updates
cases.code:
count = 2
count += 3
count += 3
print(count)

blocks.text: Code and notes do different jobs
A .py script contains Python statements. A .ipynb notebook can contain executable code cells and Markdown notes. Comments beginning with # explain code without performing a calculation.

cases.label: A comment
cases.code:
amount = 7
# amount = 100
print(amount)

cases.label: An assignment
cases.code:
amount = 7
amount = 100
print(amount)

blocks.text: Rebuild from a clean start
Restart the kernel and run the code cells from top to bottom to check a notebook's dependencies. A calculation that needs an old, unrecorded variable will fail after the restart.

cases.label: Complete sequence
cases.code:
units = 3
cost = 8
total = units * cost

cases.label: Changed input
cases.code:
units = 5
cost = 8
total = units * cost

lessons.title: Know what a number means

blocks.text: Digits can still be text
Quotation marks make a string. Adding two strings joins their characters. Convert valid numeric text with int or float before doing arithmetic.

cases.label: Text
cases.code:
a = '12'
b = '3'
result = a + b

cases.label: Numbers
cases.code:
a = '12'
b = '3'
result = int(a) + int(b)

blocks.text: Division has two answers
The / operator performs true division. The // operator takes the floor of the quotient, including for negative values. The remainder % completes a = (a // b) * b + a % b.

cases.label: Positive dividend
cases.code:
a = 11
b = 4
quotient = a // b
remainder = a % b
exact = a / b

cases.label: Negative dividend
cases.code:
a = -11
b = 4
quotient = a // b
remainder = a % b
exact = a / b

blocks.text: Precision depends on the type

Python integers can grow beyond a fixed 32-bit range, subject to available memory. Floats approximate many decimal fractions. For decimal money, use a suitable decimal representation rather than assuming every float is exact.

cases.label: Large integer
cases.code:
value = 2 ** 40
exact = value + 1

cases.label: Decimal float
cases.code:
total = 0.1 + 0.2
equal = total == 0.3

blocks.text: Truth is not a word
False is a Boolean value. The string 'False' contains characters and is truthy because it is nonempty. Test the condition you mean instead of relying on the spelling of a string.

cases.label: Boolean
cases.code:
value = False
flag = bool(value)

cases.label: Nonempty text
cases.code:
value = 'False'
flag = bool(value)

lessons.orientation: Separate numeric values from text and choose arithmetic deliberately.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Take exactly the text you need

blocks.text: The boundary belongs between characters
Index zero is the first character. Slices include the start and stop before the end: label[1:4] contains positions 1, 2 and 3.

cases.label: Middle slice
cases.code:
label = 'PLANET'
part = label[1:4]

cases.label: Last characters
cases.code:
label = 'PLANET'
part = label[-2:]

blocks.text: A method returns new text
Strings are immutable. Methods such as strip and upper return a new string; they do not rewrite the original. Assign the result when you want to keep it.

cases.label: Keep the result
cases.code:
name = '  bay  '
clean = name.strip().upper()

cases.label: Ignore the result
cases.code:
name = '  bay  '
name.strip().upper()

blocks.text: Escapes represent characters
Inside a string, backslash-n represents a newline character. It counts as one character even though its source spelling uses two. print displays the line break.

cases.label: Line break
cases.code:
text = 'red\nblue'
size = len(text)
print(text)

cases.label: Literal backslash
cases.code:
text = r'red\nblue'
size = len(text)
print(text)

blocks.text: Slices tolerate an early end
A slice can end beyond the available text and simply stops at the end. A single index outside the string raises IndexError. Empty and shorter inputs deserve explicit checks.

cases.label: Longer input
cases.code:
code = 'ABCDEF'
tail = code[3:20]

cases.label: Shorter input
cases.code:
code = 'AB'
tail = code[3:20]

lessons.orientation: Use zero-based indexing, slice boundaries and string methods.
lessons.reviewLabel: Take exactly the text you need

lessons.title: Change a collection without surprises

blocks.text: Two names can share one list
Assigning b = a makes both names refer to the same list. Appending through either name changes that shared object. Assignment does not automatically copy a collection.

cases.label: Shared list
cases.code:
a = [2, 5]
b = a
b.append(8)

cases.label: Separate outer list
cases.code:
a = [2, 5]
b = a.copy()
b.append(8)

blocks.text: Append changes the list
append adds one item in place and returns None. Do not replace a list with the return value of append. Use the list after calling the method.

cases.label: Keep the list
cases.code:
items = [4, 7]
result = items.append(9)

cases.label: Overwrite the name
cases.code:
items = [4, 7]
items = items.append(9)

blocks.text: A copy can still share inner objects
list.copy makes a shallow copy. The outer list is new, but nested mutable objects are still shared. A tuple prevents replacing its own items; it does not freeze a list stored inside it.

cases.label: Nested list copy
cases.code:
a = [[1], [2]]
b = a.copy()
b[0].append(3)

cases.label: List inside a tuple
cases.code:
record = ('Bay', [1, 2])
record[1].append(3)

blocks.text: Slicing chooses positions
List slices use the same start-inclusive, stop-exclusive boundaries as strings. Repeating a list with * repeats its contents; it does not multiply each number.

cases.label: Slice
cases.code:
values = [3, 6, 9, 12]
result = values[1:3]

cases.label: Repeat
cases.code:
values = [3, 6]
result = values * 2

lessons.orientation: Follow list aliases, shallow copies, append and tuple immutability.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Choose the right collection

blocks.text: Keys identify values
A dictionary maps unique keys to values. Assigning a value to an existing key replaces that entry. It does not add another copy of the key.

cases.label: Replace a value
cases.code:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}
stock['pen'] = 7

cases.label: Add a key
cases.code:
stock = {'pen': 3, 'book': 2}
stock['lamp'] = 7

blocks.text: Membership asks about keys
The expression key in mapping checks dictionary keys. To test the values, use mapping.values(). get lets you specify a fallback for an absent key without raising KeyError.

cases.label: Key lookup
Value lookup

blocks.text: Distinct items form a set
A set removes duplicate elements and has no sequence position. Built-in set is mutable; add and remove change it. frozenset provides an immutable set.

cases.label: Remove duplicates
cases.code:
visits = ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay']
shops = set(visits)

cases.label: Add a member
cases.code:
shops = {'Bay', 'Hill'}
shops.add('Lake')

blocks.text: Compare membership
Set intersection & keeps members in both sets. Union | keeps members in either. Difference - keeps members in the left set that are absent from the right.

lessons.orientation: Use dictionary keys for lookup and sets for distinct membership.

lessons.title: Control which work happens

blocks.text: Only the matching branch runs
An if/elif/else chain chooses the first true condition. Put specific conditions before broader ones when their ranges overlap. Equality == compares values; = assigns a name.

cases.label: Small order
Large order

blocks.text: A range excludes its stop
for takes each item in turn. range(start, stop, step) excludes stop. Initialise an accumulator before the loop and update it inside the indented body.

cases.label: First four integers
cases.code:
items = list(range(4))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

cases.label: Odd values
cases.code:
items = list(range(1, 8, 2))
total = 0
for item in items:
    total += item

blocks.text: A while loop needs progress
while tests its condition before each iteration. An update must eventually make the condition false when you intend the loop to finish. The final value may cross the threshold.

cases.label: Add two
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 2
    turns += 1

cases.label: Add three
cases.code:
count = 1
turns = 0
while count < 6:
    count += 3
    turns += 1

blocks.text: Choose logical or bit operations
and, or and not combine scalar truth tests. On integers, & and | operate on bits. Pandas later uses & and | for elementwise Boolean masks, with parentheses around each comparison.

cases.label: Logical test
cases.code:
x = 6
within = x > 3 and x < 9

cases.label: Integer bits
cases.code:
a = 6
b = 3
both_bits = a & b

lessons.orientation: Trace branches, ranges, loop updates and Boolean conditions.

lessons.title: Turn a calculation into a tool

blocks.text: Return a useful value
A function groups statements under a name. Its parameters receive arguments when you call it. return sends a value back to the caller; print only writes output.

cases.label: Return
Print

blocks.text: Name the argument you mean
A default argument supplies a value when the caller omits it. Keyword arguments make the intended parameter explicit. They can be supplied in a different order from the function definition.

cases.label: Default rate
Named arguments

blocks.text: A parameter can refer to a mutable object
A function can mutate a list passed to it because the parameter refers to that object. Rebinding a local parameter to a new list does not replace the caller's name.

cases.label: Mutate the list
cases.code:
def add_item(items):
    items.append(9)
values = [1, 2]
add_item(values)

cases.label: Rebind a parameter
cases.code:
def add_item(items):
    items = [9]
values = [1, 2]
add_item(values)

blocks.text: Import brings a module into scope

A package must be available in the interpreter's environment before import can use it. An alias is a shorter local name. Importing a library does not install it, and a notebook may use a different environment from a terminal.

cases.label: Module name
cases.code:
import math
result = math.sqrt(81)

cases.label: Alias
cases.code:
import math as m
result = m.sqrt(81)

lessons.orientation: Define functions, pass arguments, return values and import installed libraries.

lessons.title: Handle failure without hiding it

blocks.text: Expect a specific failure
int can parse a valid integer string. Invalid text raises ValueError. Catch that expected exception and choose an explicit fallback or report the bad input.

cases.label: Valid text
Invalid text

blocks.text: Record what was skipped
Skipping an invalid row changes the population being analysed. Keep a rejection count and make the policy explicit. A catch-all exception can hide programming mistakes.

cases.label: All valid
One bad value

blocks.text: Close a resource when the block ends

with manages entry and exit for a resource. When used with open, it closes the file after the block, even if the block exits through an exception. These examples use in-memory text streams so no local files are changed.

cases.label: Read lines
cases.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('Bay\nHill\n') as stream:
    lines = stream.readlines()
closed = stream.closed

cases.label: Count characters
cases.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('Lake') as stream:
    text = stream.read()
size = len(text)
closed = stream.closed

blocks.text: Locate data explicitly

A relative path is resolved from the working directory, which may differ from the script's directory. Check the intended location and encoding when reading files. A missing file and invalid numeric text are different failures.

cases.label: Line endings
cases.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('3\n7\n') as stream:
    values = [int(line.strip()) for line in stream]
total = sum(values)

cases.label: Blank line policy
cases.code:
from io import StringIO
with StringIO('3\n\n7\n') as stream:
    values = [int(line) for line in stream if line.strip()]
total = sum(values)

lessons.orientation: Catch expected exceptions and manage files with a context manager.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Give data a shape

blocks.text: A list and an array behave differently
A Python list is a general sequence. A NumPy array stores elements using a dtype and supports elementwise arithmetic. Multiplying a list repeats it; multiplying a numeric array scales its values.

cases.label: Python list
cases.code:
values = [2, 4, 6]
result = values * 2

cases.label: NumPy array
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.array([2, 4, 6])
result = values * 2

blocks.text: Shape counts each axis
The shape of a two-dimensional array gives rows first, then columns. size counts all elements. ndim counts the number of axes, not the number of stored values.

cases.label: Two by three
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(2, 3)
shape = a.shape
size = a.size

cases.label: Three by two
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(6).reshape(3, 2)
shape = a.shape
size = a.size

blocks.text: Reshape preserves the element count
reshape changes the arrangement without changing how many elements there are. The product of the requested dimensions must equal size. A single -1 lets NumPy infer the remaining dimension.

cases.label: Infer columns
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(3, -1)

cases.label: Infer rows
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.arange(12)
result = a.reshape(-1, 2)

blocks.text: A dtype is a storage choice
NumPy integer dtypes have fixed widths. That differs from Python's arbitrary-precision int. Choose a dtype suited to the expected range rather than assuming all integers grow automatically.

cases.label: 16-bit storage
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int16)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

cases.label: 64-bit storage
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([12, 30], dtype=np.int64)
bytes_per_item = a.itemsize

lessons.orientation: Build NumPy arrays and track dimensions, shape and element counts.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Calculate across the right axis

blocks.text: An operation reaches every element
Arithmetic between equal-shaped arrays acts on matching positions. Arithmetic with a scalar broadcasts that scalar across all elements.

cases.label: Add a scalar
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 8])
result = a + 3

cases.label: Multiply positions
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 8])
b = np.array([1, 2, 3])
result = a * b

blocks.text: Reduce rows to column totals
For a two-dimensional array, sum(axis=0) combines values down the row axis, leaving one result per column. sum(axis=1) combines columns within each row.

cases.label: Down the columns
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=0)

cases.label: Across each row
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
result = a.sum(axis=1)

blocks.text: Broadcast only compatible shapes
A one-dimensional array matching the final dimension can be combined with every row. NumPy compares dimensions from the right; each pair must match or one must be 1.

cases.label: Column offsets
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + np.array([10, 20])

cases.label: One offset everywhere
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([[1, 2], [3, 4]])
result = a + 10

blocks.text: A slice may share storage
A basic NumPy slice usually views the original storage. Editing the view can change the original array. Use copy when you need an independent array.

cases.label: View
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2]
b[0] = 99

cases.label: Copy
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.array([2, 4, 6])
b = a[:2].copy()
b[0] = 99

lessons.orientation: Apply elementwise operations, broadcasting and reductions.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Generate values with clear boundaries

blocks.text: arange stops before the boundary
arange(start, stop, step) produces a spacing sequence and excludes stop. For integer steps, reason about the last value strictly before that boundary.

cases.label: Start at zero
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(5)

cases.label: Choose start and step
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.arange(2, 12, 3)

blocks.text: linspace chooses a count
linspace uses the requested number of evenly spaced samples. It includes both endpoints by default. With endpoint=False, the final boundary is excluded and the spacing changes.

cases.label: Include the endpoint
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4)

cases.label: Exclude the endpoint
cases.code:
import numpy as np
values = np.linspace(0, 12, 4, endpoint=False)

blocks.text: A random upper bound is usually exclusive
Generator.integers(low, high) includes low and excludes high by default. To simulate a six-sided die, use low=1 and high=7. A seed makes this demonstration reproducible in the recorded environment.

cases.label: Die outcomes
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(21)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

cases.label: Different seed
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(22)
draws = rng.integers(1, 7, size=6)

blocks.text: Repeat a run, not a guarantee

Resetting the same generator seed and repeating the same operations reproduces a sequence in the same environment. Repeated draws without resetting advance the generator. Reproducibility does not prove that a sample represents a population.

cases.label: Reset the seed
cases.code:
import numpy as np
a = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
b = np.random.default_rng(9).integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

cases.label: Advance the generator
cases.code:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
a = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
b = rng.integers(0, 10, 4)
equal = np.array_equal(a, b)

lessons.orientation: Distinguish arange, linspace and reproducible random draws.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Meet a real table

blocks.text: Read rows and name columns
read_csv turns delimited text into a DataFrame. The header normally supplies column names; each data line becomes a row. In these examples, StringIO provides an in-memory text file.

cases.label: Comma separated
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
csv = 'shop,units\nBay,2\nHill,5'
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv))

cases.label: Semicolon separated
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
csv = 'shop;units\nBay;2\nHill;5'
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO(csv), sep=';')

blocks.text: Inspect before calculating
shape reports rows and columns. head shows initial rows without changing the table. A selected column is usually a Series; selecting a list of column names keeps a DataFrame.

cases.label: A Series
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df['units']
shape = df.shape

cases.label: A DataFrame
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[['units']]
shape = result.shape

blocks.text: Identifiers are not measurements
A code such as 0012 may look numeric but depend on its leading zeros. Specify a string dtype for identifiers instead of relying on numeric inference. Check inferred dtypes before analysis.

cases.label: Inferred numeric ID
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO('code,units\n0012,4\n0013,7'))

cases.label: Explicit text ID
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO
df = pd.read_csv(StringIO('code,units\n0012,4\n0013,7'), dtype={'code': 'str'})

blocks.text: Match the reader to the source

read_excel can select a worksheet with sheet_name; read_csv selects parsing rules for a text file. A CSV has no worksheets. Methods such as columns, dtypes and head help confirm that the import matches its source.

cases.label: Column names
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
names = list(df.columns)
preview = df.head(2)

cases.label: Column types
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
types = df.dtypes.astype(str)

values.name: types
values.display:
shop       str
units    int64
price    int64
dtype: str

lessons.orientation: Read CSV data, inspect a DataFrame and preserve meaningful column types.
lessons.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

lessons.title: Find the intended row

blocks.text: A label is not a position
loc looks up index labels. iloc uses zero-based positions. With index labels 10, 20 and 30, the first row has label 10 and position 0.

cases.label: Label 20
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[20, 'units']

cases.label: Position 1
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[1, 0]

blocks.text: Label slices include the stop
On this sorted index, loc[10:20] includes both existing boundary labels. iloc[0:1] includes position 0 and stops before position 1. Do not transfer one slicing convention to the other.

cases.label: Label slice
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.loc[10:20]

cases.label: Position slice
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])
result = df.iloc[0:1]

blocks.text: Choose rows and columns together
The expression before the comma selects rows; the expression after it selects columns. loc accepts column names, while iloc accepts column positions.

cases.label: Named columns
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 5, 8], 'price': [4, 6, 3]}, index=[10, 20, 30])

lessons.title: Keep unknown separate from zero

blocks.text: Missing is a different observation
pandas uses missing-value markers suited to the dtype, such as NaN, NaT or pd.NA. Use isna to detect missing data. An observed zero is a known value and must not be treated as missing.

cases.label: Numeric observations
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([0, None, 8], dtype='Float64')
missing = s.isna()

cases.label: Count missing
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([None, 4, None], dtype='Float64')
count = s.isna().sum()

blocks.text: The denominator can change
Many numeric reductions skip missing values by default. count counts known values; size counts all positions. mean uses the known observations unless you choose a different explicit policy.

cases.label: Keep unknown
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, None, 8], dtype='Float64')
known = s.count()
mean = s.mean()

cases.label: Replace with zero
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([2, None, 8], dtype='Float64')
filled = s.fillna(0)
mean = filled.mean()

blocks.text: A fill value asserts something

fillna(0) claims that unknown values should count as zero. That may be justified for some measurements and false for others. Preserve the original data and document the policy before replacing missing values.

lessons.title: Turn messy text into usable columns

blocks.text: Clean one value at a time across a column
The .str accessor applies string operations to a Series. strip removes outside whitespace; lower standardises letter case. These operations return new values for explicit assignment.

cases.label: Original labels

result = s.str.strip()

result = s.str.strip().str.lower()

blocks.text: Split a known structure

str.split with expand=True returns separate columns. Choose the delimiter from the data and limit splits when the remaining text may also contain it. A fixed two-part example does not prove every input has two parts.

parts = s.str.split('|', n=1, expand=True)

blocks.text: Choose the simplest transformation
Series.map can call a function for each value. A lambda is a small function expression. Prefer an available vectorised string or arithmetic operation when it expresses the same calculation clearly.

cases.label: Map a function

import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series(['red,blue', 'green'])
counts = s.map(lambda text: len(text.split(',')))

blocks.text: Rows need an explicit axis
DataFrame.apply(..., axis=1) passes each row to the function. Its default axis=0 passes each column instead. Rename columns with a mapping and keep the returned table.

cases.label: Apply by row

df['total'] = df.apply(lambda row: row['a'] + row['b'], axis=1)

lessons.title: Read a date without guessing

blocks.text: State the expected date format
A string such as 03/04/2026 is ambiguous without a format convention. Supply format when the source format is known, then inspect failures instead of silently choosing an interpretation.

cases.label: Day first
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['03/04/2026'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%d/%m/%Y')

cases.label: Month first
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['03/04/2026'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%m/%d/%Y')

blocks.text: An invalid date stays visible
errors='coerce' converts unparseable dates to NaT. Count and inspect those missing dates. Assigning a made-up date can distort trends and durations.

cases.label: Valid calendar dates
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['2026-02-28', '2026-03-01'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce')

cases.label: Impossible date
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
raw = pd.Series(['2026-02-30', '2026-03-01'])
dates = pd.to_datetime(raw, format='%Y-%m-%d', errors='coerce')
invalid = dates.isna().sum()

blocks.text: An epoch number needs a unit

Unix timestamps commonly count seconds from 1970-01-01 UTC, but datasets also use milliseconds and other units. Supply unit explicitly when converting. An integer representation of a datetime is not automatically seconds.

cases.label: Seconds
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([0, 60]), unit='s', utc=True)

cases.label: Milliseconds
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series([0, 60]), unit='ms', utc=True)

blocks.text: Extract or subtract dates deliberately
The .dt accessor extracts calendar fields from a datetime Series. Subtracting timestamps produces a duration. Keep timezone assumptions consistent before comparing events.

cases.label: Calendar month
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2026-04-02', '2026-05-03']))
months = dates.dt.month

cases.label: Elapsed days
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
dates = pd.to_datetime(pd.Series(['2026-04-02', '2026-04-05']))
days = (dates.iloc[1] - dates.iloc[0]).days

blocks.text: A summary has a denominator
mean averages the known numeric values; median identifies their middle. describe supplies several descriptive statistics. A count is only meaningful when you know what can be missing.

lessons.title: Combine data without multiplying the answer

blocks.text: Stacking keeps duplicate rows
concat stacks rows by default and aligns columns by name. ignore_index=True creates a fresh positional index. It does not deduplicate records; this is closer to SQL UNION ALL than UNION.

cases.label: Preserve labels
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 4]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'units': [4, 6]})
result = pd.concat([a, b])

cases.label: Fresh row labels
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
a = pd.DataFrame({'units': [2, 4]})
b = pd.DataFrame({'units': [4, 6]})
result = pd.concat([a, b], ignore_index=True)

blocks.text: A left join keeps unmatched left rows
An inner merge keeps matching keys. A left merge retains every left row and supplies missing right-side values when there is no match. The how argument determines which rule runs.

cases.label: Inner matches

people = pd.DataFrame({'customer': [1, 2, 4], 'region': ['East', 'West', 'East']})
result = orders.merge(people, on='customer', how='inner', validate='many_to_one')

lessons.title: Change the layout without losing the meaning

blocks.text: A pivot needs one value per cell
pivot maps an index key and a column key to one value. The pair must uniquely identify the value. Wide layout can make comparisons easier to read while preserving the underlying observations.

cases.label: Shops across months
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Jan', 'Feb'], 'units': [2, 5, 3, 7]})
result = df.pivot(index='shop', columns='month', values='units')

values.name: result

shop

Hill     7    3

blocks.text: Duplicates require an aggregation rule
pivot_table can aggregate repeated index-column pairs. Specify aggfunc deliberately: its default mean and a chosen sum answer different questions.

df = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Bay', 'Hill'], 'month': ['Jan', 'Jan', 'Jan'], 'units': [2, 6, 3]})

melt keeps identifier columns and turns selected value columns into a variable column and a value column. Melting two measurement columns for each of three rows produces six long-form rows.

blocks.text: State what one row means
Each row in this dataset is one order, identified by id. Check duplicate identifiers before joining or aggregating. Repeated shop names are expected because a shop can receive several orders.

cases.label: Order identifiers

import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
duplicate_ids = orders['id'].duplicated().sum()
rows = len(orders)

blocks.text: Qualify the population and its missing data
The report counts paid orders only. One paid order has an unknown price. Keep that count visible and call the result known revenue; replacing the unknown price with zero would hide uncertainty.

blocks.text: Validate the enrichment
Join each order to at most one shop-region record, then inspect unmatched rows. many_to_one validation catches a repeated lookup key before it can inflate revenue.

cases.label: Complete lookup

import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
lookup = pd.DataFrame({'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Lake'], 'region': ['East', 'West', 'East']})
result = orders.merge(lookup, on='shop', how='left', validate='many_to_one')

blocks.text: Report the result and the caveat together
Group the paid population, total known revenue and retain the number of unknown prices. Sort for comparison. The final table communicates what is measured and what remains unknown.

cases.label: Revenue with its caveat
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
paid = orders[orders['paid']].copy()
paid['revenue'] = paid['units'] * paid['price']
paid['unknown_price'] = paid['price'].isna()
result = paid.groupby('shop', as_index=False).agg(known_revenue=('revenue', lambda s: s.sum(min_count=1)), unknown_prices=('unknown_price', 'sum'))

cases.label: Correct the missing input
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.DataFrame({'id': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake', 'Hill'], 'units': [2, 3, 4, 1, 2], 'price': [5, 8, None, 6, 8], 'paid': [True, True, True, False, True]})
orders.loc[orders['id'] == 3, 'price'] = 5
paid = orders[orders['paid']].copy()
paid['revenue'] = paid['units'] * paid['price']
result = paid.groupby('shop', as_index=False)['revenue'].sum()

The displayed Series order is b followed by a.
Read the value paired with label a, not the first displayed value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The value with label a is 22, regardless of its position in the Series.

questions.prompt: For units [1, 4, 6, 2], how many rows pass units >= 4?
hints: Evaluate the threshold for each row.
Test >= 4 on each value separately.
Count true comparisons, including a value equal to 4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only 4 and 6 satisfy the comparison.

questions.prompt: Rows are (Bay, 2), (Bay, 5), (Hill, 7). How many pass shop == 'Bay' AND units > 3?
hints: Both comparisons must be true for the same row.
First identify Bay rows.
Among those rows, count only the ones with units greater than 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the Bay row with 5 units passes both conditions.

questions.prompt: Which expression combines two pandas Boolean comparisons safely?
hints: Use the elementwise operator and preserve each comparison.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Parenthesised comparisons joined by & form an elementwise AND mask.

questions.prompt: Which update directly targets df?
hints: Keep the row and column selection in one assignment.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A single loc assignment targets rows and a column on df. Chained indexing can target a separate object.

questions.prompt: Units are [2, 3] and prices [7, 5]. What is total revenue from units * price?
hints: Multiply matching positions, then sum.
Revenue is calculated for each row before summing.
Calculate 2 * 7 + 3 * 5.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row revenues are 14 and 15, totalling 29.

questions.prompt: A five-row DataFrame receives df['fee'] = 3. What is df['fee'].sum()?
hints: The assignment applies to every row.
A scalar column assignment repeats the value for every row.
Add five identical fees of 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The scalar fills all five rows; 5 × 3 = 15.

questions.prompt: How many entries are missing in [0, None, 4, None]?
hints: Do not count zero as missing.
Only the missing markers count here.
Count the None entries and leave 0 as a known observation.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The two None entries are missing. Zero is an observed value.

questions.prompt: What is the default mean of [4, missing, 10] in a numeric pandas Series?
hints: Exclude the missing entry from both sum and count.
The missing entry does not enter the sum or denominator.
Add the two known values and divide by two.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known values 4 and 10 have mean 14 ÷ 2 = 7.

questions.prompt: What assumption does filling an unknown measurement with zero make?
hints: Separate a chosen replacement from an observation.

acceptedIdeas: That the missing measurement should count as an observed zero
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A zero fill changes the data used in calculations. It does not recover the unknown original value.

choices.label: That the original value has been recovered
That missingness can no longer affect analysis
That the missing measurement should count as an observed zero

questions.prompt: Which expression detects pandas missing values?
hints: Use pandas' missing-value operation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: isna detects the dtype's missing-value marker. Zero and the string 'missing' are ordinary values unless a parsing policy says otherwise.

questions.prompt: What is the mean after filling [3, missing, 9] with zero?
hints: The replacement now participates in the denominator.
After filling, all three positions are known values.
Calculate (3 + 0 + 9) / 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The filled values are 3, 0 and 9; 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

questions.prompt: A Series contains [1, missing, missing, 7, 0]. What does count() return?
hints: count excludes missing values but includes zero.
count includes every nonmissing position.
Cross out the missing markers and count the remaining entries.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known values are 1, 7 and 0, so count returns 3.

questions.prompt: How many characters remain in '  NORTH '.strip().lower()?
hints: Trim outside whitespace before counting.
Case conversion changes letters without adding characters.
Remove surrounding whitespace and count the remaining letters.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The cleaned string is north, which has five characters.

questions.prompt: Splitting each of two strings once with expand=True produces two columns. How many data cells are in the result?
hints: Keep the row count separate from the split-field count.
Every source row contributes one cell to each split column.
Multiply the number of source strings by two columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two rows times two columns gives four cells.

questions.prompt: What does Series.map(lambda x: len(x)) pass to the function?
hints: Identify which object owns the method.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Series.map applies the function to each value in that Series.

questions.prompt: Which apply argument passes DataFrame rows to a function?
hints: Choose the rowwise axis.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: DataFrame.apply with axis=1 calls the function on each row. The default axis=0 works on columns.

questions.prompt: For 'red,blue,gold', what does len(text.split(',')) produce?
hints: Count parts rather than delimiters.
Each separator divides adjacent parts.
Write the strings between commas and count the parts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Splitting at the two commas produces three items.

questions.prompt: A row has a = 7 and b = 9. What is row['a'] + row['b']?
hints: Use the two values from the same row.
axis=1 means both operands come from the same row.
Add the row's a value to its b value.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The row calculation adds 7 and 9 to give 16.

questions.prompt: Parse '05/09/2026' with format='%d/%m/%Y'. What month number results?
hints: Follow the specified format rather than a regional guess.
%d is day and %m is month.
Read the middle field as the month number.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The format reads day 05 and month 09, so the month is 9.

questions.prompt: With format='%Y-%m-%d' and errors='coerce', how many missing dates result from ['2026-02-30', '2026-03-01', 'bad']?
hints: Check calendar validity as well as formatting.
Both an impossible calendar day and unrecognisable text fail parsing.
Count entries that cannot become dates under the given format.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: February 30 and bad cannot be parsed as valid dates, so both become NaT.

questions.prompt: Which parameter distinguishes an epoch count in seconds from milliseconds?
hints: The number alone does not specify its scale.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: unit tells pandas how to interpret the numeric offset from the epoch.

questions.prompt: What is the result of coercing an invalid datetime?
hints: Coercion records a failed parse as missing.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: NaT marks the missing datetime. It does not supply a valid replacement date.

questions.prompt: How many seconds separate epoch offsets 120 and 300 when unit='s'?
hints: Subtract offsets in the same unit.
Both offsets use the same unit.
Subtract the earlier epoch offset from the later one.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both offsets use seconds, so the elapsed time is 300 − 120 = 180 seconds.

questions.prompt: How many days separate 2026-06-02 and 2026-06-07 at the same time of day?
hints: Subtract the earlier date from the later date.
The times of day are equal.
Count elapsed midnight-to-midnight intervals between the two dates.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The later date is five days after the earlier one.

questions.prompt: What is the mean of [2, 4, 6, 20]?
hints: Use the sum and the observation count.
All four observations are known.
Add the values and divide their sum by four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The values sum to 32; dividing by four gives 8.

questions.prompt: Rows are (Bay, 2), (Hill, 3), (Bay, 6). What is Bay's grouped sum?
hints: Keep only the requested group's observations.
The Hill row belongs to a different group.
Add the two values attached to Bay.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The Bay rows contribute 2 and 6, giving 8.

questions.prompt: A group has five rows, with two missing units. What does units.count() count?
hints: Identify which operation counts observations versus known values.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: count excludes missing unit values. size would count all five rows.

questions.prompt: How can a group with a missing key be retained?
hints: Control the treatment of the grouping key.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: dropna=False retains missing grouping keys as a group without inventing numeric measurements.

choices.label: Fill every numeric column with zero

questions.prompt: What is the median of [1, 3, 5, 21]?
hints: Sort and inspect the two middle positions.
There are an even number of observations.
Average the second and third values in the sorted list.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The middle values are 3 and 5, so the median is their average, 4.

questions.prompt: What is nunique() for ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Lake']?
hints: Repeated labels count once.
Repeated shop names collapse to one distinct value.
List each different name once, then count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There are three distinct shop labels.

questions.prompt: Concatenate a three-row table and a four-row table without deduplication. How many rows result?
hints: concat does not remove repeated rows.
No row-removal operation is requested.
Add the row counts of both inputs.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Row stacking keeps all 3 + 4 = 7 rows.

questions.prompt: Left keys are [1, 2, 3] and unique right keys are [1, 2]. How many rows does a left merge return?
hints: The right keys are unique, so matching does not multiply left rows.
Every left key has at most one matching right row.
Count all left rows, including the unmatched key.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: All three left rows remain. Key 3 receives missing right-side values.

questions.prompt: Which validation asserts that the lookup table on the right has unique keys?
hints: The right side is the one in many-to-one.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: many_to_one permits repeated left keys but requires each right key to identify at most one row.

questions.prompt: How does pandas merge handle a null key on both sides?
hints: Check the library's missing-key rule.

acceptedIdeas: It can match the null keys
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pandas can match null keys. Do not assume the usual SQL equality-join treatment of NULL.

choices.label: It can match the null keys
It converts both keys to zero

questions.prompt: One key occurs three times on the left and twice on the right. How many matched rows does that key produce?
hints: Count all matching pairs.
Each of the left occurrences matches every right occurrence.
Multiply the number of left and right occurrences of this key.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each left row pairs with each right row: 3 × 2 = 6.

questions.prompt: Left keys are [1, 1, 2, 3] and unique right keys are [1, 2]. How many rows does an inner merge return?
hints: Count matching left rows, including repeated keys.
Each left occurrence of a matching key produces one row here.
Cross out the left key absent from the right, then count the remaining occurrences.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Both left rows with key 1 and the row with key 2 match. Key 3 is excluded.

questions.prompt: A complete pivot has three shops and four month columns. How many measurement cells does it contain?
hints: Count the grid cells without the labels.
Labels are not measurement cells.
Multiply the number of shops by the number of month columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the three shops has four monthly cells, giving 12.

questions.prompt: Two Bay/Jan records have units 3 and 9. What cell value does pivot_table(..., aggfunc='sum') produce?
hints: Apply the specified aggregation.
Both records map to the same output cell.
Apply sum to their two unit values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The duplicate key pair is aggregated as 3 + 9 = 12.

questions.prompt: Why does pivot fail when one index-column pair has two records?
hints: One output cell needs a single value.

acceptedIdeas: The requested cell is not uniquely identified
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pivot does not choose an aggregation for ambiguous cells. Resolve duplicates or use an explicit pivot_table aggregation.

choices.label: The requested cell is not uniquely identified
The table must have at least ten rows

questions.prompt: Which melt argument identifies columns that stay attached to every measurement?
hints: Keep the identifier alongside each resulting observation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: id_vars retains identifier columns while selected value columns are unpivoted.

questions.prompt: A four-row table melts three measurement columns. How many long-form rows result?
hints: Count one result row per selected measurement cell.
Each original row supplies three selected measurements.
Multiply the original row count by the number of melted value columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each original row contributes three measurements, producing 4 × 3 = 12 rows.

questions.prompt: Repeated records have values 4 and 10. What does aggfunc='mean' produce?
hints: The selected operation is mean, not sum.
The rule is mean instead of sum.
Add the two values, then divide by their count.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The mean is (4 + 10) ÷ 2 = 7.

questions.prompt: Order IDs are [1, 2, 2, 3]. How many rows does duplicated() flag after the first occurrence?
hints: Count extra occurrences, not every row sharing the key.
The first occurrence of each ID is kept unflagged.
Count only the later repeated occurrence.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only the second occurrence of ID 2 is flagged with the default keep='first'.

questions.prompt: Paid flags are [True, False, True, True]. How many orders belong in the paid report?
hints: Define the population before aggregating.
The paid flag defines which rows belong in the population.
Count true flags and exclude false flags.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three rows have a true paid flag.

questions.prompt: A paid order has an unknown price. Which report label preserves that limitation?
hints: Do not turn an unknown measurement into a known zero.

acceptedIdeas: Known revenue, with the unknown-price count
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Known revenue reports the measured amount while the missing-price count states what the total excludes.

choices.label: Revenue after silently replacing the price with zero
Known revenue, with the unknown-price count

questions.prompt: A shop lookup contains two records for the same shop. What should a many-to-one enrichment do?
hints: Check the expected relationship between order rows and lookup keys.

acceptedIdeas: Reject the ambiguous lookup and resolve it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Validate the lookup before reporting. Resolve the duplicate according to its meaning rather than multiplying orders.

choices.label: Reject the ambiguous lookup and resolve it
Duplicate each order and continue silently

questions.prompt: Paid orders are 2 units at 7, 3 units at 5, and 4 units at an unknown price. What is known revenue?
hints: Sum only the two known products.
The unknown-price row has no known revenue contribution.
Calculate 2 * 7 + 3 * 5; retain the missing-price caveat.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The known rows contribute 14 and 15, totalling 29. The unknown row remains a caveat.

questions.prompt: Paid orders contain 2 units at 7, 3 units at 5, and 4 units at a newly confirmed price of 6. What is the complete revenue?
hints: Add the newly established contribution.
The third row now has a confirmed price.
Calculate 2 * 7 + 3 * 5 + 4 * 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The missing order adds 4 × 6 = 24 to the known 29, producing 53.

flashcards.front: Set a = 7, then b = a + 2, then a = 1. What is b?
flashcards.back: b keeps the value 9 assigned before a changed.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: b keeps the value 9 assigned before a changed.

flashcards.front: What notebook component retains Python variables between code-cell runs?
flashcards.back: The kernel retains the live Python state until it is restarted or shut down.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The kernel retains the live Python state until it is restarted or shut down.

flashcards.front: What is -8 // 3?
flashcards.back: Flooring -2.666… gives -3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Flooring -2.666… gives -3.

flashcards.front: Which Python built-in type stores a whole number with arbitrary precision?
flashcards.back: int stores arbitrary-precision integers; available memory still limits their size.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: int stores arbitrary-precision integers; available memory still limits their size.

flashcards.front: How many characters are in 'SPECTRUM'[1:6]?
flashcards.back: Positions 1 through 5 are included; position 6 is excluded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Positions 1 through 5 are included; position 6 is excluded.

flashcards.front: What string method removes surrounding whitespace? Give the method name without parentheses.
flashcards.back: strip returns a new string with leading and trailing whitespace removed.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: strip returns a new string with leading and trailing whitespace removed.

flashcards.front: x = [5]; y = x; y.extend([6, 7]). How many items are in x?
flashcards.back: The shared list becomes [5, 6, 7].

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The shared list becomes [5, 6, 7].

flashcards.front: What immutable Python sequence commonly groups a fixed record?
flashcards.back: A tuple is an immutable sequence, although mutable objects held inside it can still change.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A tuple is an immutable sequence, although mutable objects held inside it can still change.

flashcards.front: How many members are in {2, 4, 6} - {4, 8}?
flashcards.back: Removing shared member 4 leaves 2 and 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Removing shared member 4 leaves 2 and 6.

flashcards.front: What dictionary method returns a fallback when a key is absent? Give its name.
flashcards.back: get(key, default) returns the mapped value or the specified default.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: get(key, default) returns the mapped value or the specified default.

flashcards.front: How many iterations does for x in range(3, 12, 3) perform?
flashcards.back: The values are 3, 6 and 9; 12 is excluded.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The values are 3, 6 and 9; 12 is excluded.

flashcards.front: Which Python keyword provides an alternative condition after if?
flashcards.back: elif checks another condition if the preceding condition was false.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: elif checks another condition if the preceding condition was false.

flashcards.front: def add(a, b=3): return a + b. What is add(8, b=5)?
flashcards.back: The explicit b argument replaces the default, giving 8 + 5 = 13.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The explicit b argument replaces the default, giving 8 + 5 = 13.

flashcards.front: Which keyword sends a function's result back to its caller?
flashcards.back: return ends the function call and supplies its result.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: return ends the function call and supplies its result.

flashcards.front: Convert ['3', '?', '8'] to integers, skipping ValueError entries. What is their sum?
flashcards.back: The valid values 3 and 8 sum to 11.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The valid values 3 and 8 sum to 11.

flashcards.front: Which exception does int('apple') raise?
flashcards.back: ValueError reports that the supplied string cannot represent the requested integer.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: ValueError reports that the supplied string cannot represent the requested integer.

flashcards.front: How many elements are in np.zeros((2, 5, 3))?
flashcards.back: The size is 2 × 5 × 3 = 30.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The size is 2 × 5 × 3 = 30.

flashcards.front: Which NumPy array attribute gives its dimensions as a tuple?
flashcards.back: shape lists the length of each axis.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: shape lists the length of each axis.

flashcards.front: For [[2, 3, 4], [5, 6, 7]], what is the first row sum?
flashcards.back: The first row sums to 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The first row sums to 2 + 3 + 4 = 9.

flashcards.front: Which axis argument reduces rows to one total per column in a 2D array? Type axis= followed by the number.
flashcards.back: axis=0 reduces the row axis and leaves one value per column.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: axis=0 reduces the row axis and leaves one value per column.

flashcards.front: What is the largest value in np.arange(1, 10, 2)?
flashcards.back: The sequence is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The sequence is 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.

flashcards.front: Which NumPy function requests a number of evenly spaced samples rather than a step size?
flashcards.back: linspace selects a sample count and includes both endpoints by default.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: linspace selects a sample count and includes both endpoints by default.

flashcards.front: A DataFrame has shape (9, 4). How many data cells does it contain, excluding labels?
flashcards.back: Nine rows times four columns gives 36 data cells.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Nine rows times four columns gives 36 data cells.

flashcards.front: Which pandas reader loads comma-separated text into a DataFrame? Give the function name.
flashcards.back: pd.read_csv reads delimited text and returns a DataFrame.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pd.read_csv reads delimited text and returns a DataFrame.

flashcards.front: A five-row DataFrame uses default labels 0 through 4. How many rows does df.loc[1:3] select?
flashcards.back: Label slicing includes 1, 2 and 3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Label slicing includes 1, 2 and 3.

flashcards.front: Which selector uses labels and includes an existing stop label in a sorted slice?
flashcards.back: loc selects labels; its sorted label slices include both existing endpoints.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: loc selects labels; its sorted label slices include both existing endpoints.

flashcards.front: Values are [2, 5, 8, 11]. How many pass (x > 3) & (x < 10)?
flashcards.back: Values 5 and 8 satisfy both comparisons.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Values 5 and 8 satisfy both comparisons.

flashcards.front: Which selector supports a single explicit row-and-column assignment on a DataFrame?
flashcards.back: Use df.loc[row_mask, column_name] = value.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use df.loc[row_mask, column_name] = value.

flashcards.front: What is the default mean of [0, missing, 12, 6]?
flashcards.back: The three known observations sum to 18, giving a mean of 6.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The three known observations sum to 18, giving a mean of 6.

flashcards.front: Which Series method replaces missing values with a chosen value?
flashcards.back: fillna returns values with missing entries replaced according to an explicit policy.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: fillna returns values with missing entries replaced according to an explicit policy.

flashcards.front: A nonempty string contains three commas and no empty parts. How many parts does split(',') return?
flashcards.back: Three separators divide the string into four parts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Three separators divide the string into four parts.

flashcards.front: Which pandas accessor supplies vectorised string methods on a Series?
flashcards.back: Use the .str accessor, for example s.str.strip().

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use the .str accessor, for example s.str.strip().

flashcards.front: Parse '12/08/2026' with format='%d/%m/%Y'. What month number results?
flashcards.back: The format places the month in the middle, giving August, month 8.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The format places the month in the middle, giving August, month 8.

flashcards.front: Which datetime Series accessor exposes properties such as month and year?
flashcards.back: Use .dt, for example dates.dt.year.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Use .dt, for example dates.dt.year.

flashcards.front: A group has [2, missing, 5, missing]. What does count() return?
flashcards.back: Only 2 and 5 are known values.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Only 2 and 5 are known values.

flashcards.front: Which group aggregation counts every row, including rows with missing measurements?
flashcards.back: size counts rows; count on a column excludes its missing values.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: size counts rows; count on a column excludes its missing values.

flashcards.front: A key appears twice on each side of a merge. How many matched rows does it produce?
flashcards.back: Each of the two left rows pairs with both right rows, giving four.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the two left rows pairs with both right rows, giving four.

flashcards.front: Which pandas function stacks a list of DataFrames rowwise by default?
flashcards.back: pd.concat combines objects and retains duplicate rows unless you remove them explicitly.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: pd.concat combines objects and retains duplicate rows unless you remove them explicitly.

flashcards.front: A three-row table melts two measurement columns. How many rows result?
flashcards.back: Each source row produces two measurement rows, giving six.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each source row produces two measurement rows, giving six.

flashcards.front: Which pandas method reshapes measurement columns into variable/value rows?
flashcards.back: melt creates long-form observations while keeping the chosen identifier columns.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: melt creates long-form observations while keeping the chosen identifier columns.

flashcards.front: Known paid rows contribute 5 units at 4 and 2 units at 9. A third price is missing. What is known revenue?
flashcards.back: The observed contributions are 20 and 18, totalling 38; the unknown contribution must still be reported.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The observed contributions are 20 and 18, totalling 38; the unknown contribution must still be reported.

flashcards.front: Which merge validation allows repeated order keys on the left but requires a unique lookup on the right?
flashcards.back: validate='many_to_one' checks the lookup's key uniqueness.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: validate='many_to_one' checks the lookup's key uniqueness.
